'''Harden Marsden McConnell''' (July 18, 1927 – October 8, 2014) was an American physical chemist. His many awards included the National Medal of Science and the Wolf Prize, and he was elected to the National Academy of Science."<ref name = stanford /><ref>Keith Hodgson, Chair of the Stanford Chemistry Department, in a Departmental email message announcing Harden's death, October 10, 2014.</ref>

==Education and career==
Harden earned a B.S. degree in chemistry from [[George Washington University]] in 1947, and his Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1951 with Norman Davidson.  After serving for two years as a National Research Fellow in physics at the [[University of Chicago]] with [[Robert S. Mulliken]] and John Platt, he held a position as research chemist at Shell Development Company.  He was recruited by [[Norman Davidson (biologist)|Norman Davidson]], [[John D. Roberts]], and [[Linus Pauling]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1956 as assistant professor of chemistry, he was promoted to professor of chemistry and physics in 1963, and in 1964 he moved to [[Stanford University]] as a professor.  In 1979 he was named [[Robert E. Swain|Robert Eckles Swain]] Professor of Chemistry at Stanford University.  From September 1989 to September 1992, he was head of the department of chemistry at Stanford. On September 1, 2000, Harden was granted emeritus status.<ref name="Hayes">{{cite journal|author1=Hayes Griffith |author2=Betty J. Gaffney |author3=Alvin L. Kwiram |title=Harden M. McConnell: A Celebration of His Scientific Achievements|journal=Journal of Physical Chemistry|year=1993|volume=97|issue=12|pages=2805–2822|doi=10.1021/j100114a001}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.stanford.edu/news/2000/april12/prezreport-412.html|title=Report of the President to the Board of Trustees|website=news.stanford.edu|date=23 January 2023 }}</ref><ref>[https://chemistry.stanford.edu/faculty/harden-mcconnell "Harden M. McConnell, Professor Emeritus," Stanford Chemistry Department] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131021083419/https://chemistry.stanford.edu/faculty/harden-mcconnell |date=2013-10-21 }} (accessed October 10, 2014).</ref>

==Research==
McConnell did important research to the understanding of the relation between molecular electronic structure and electron and nuclear magnetic resonance spectra during the period of 1955 through 1965. After that, he developed the technique of spin-labels, whereby electron and nuclear magnetic resonance spectra can be used to study the structure and kinetics of proteins and membranes.<ref name="Hayes"/>

He recognized that the discovery of nuclear hyperfine interactions in aromatic free radicals represented a major breakthrough in the study of the electronic structure of unsaturated hydrocarbons. His theoretical and experimental studies of nuclear hyperfine interactions in such compounds showed conclusively that this interaction gave a measure of the unpaired electron spin densities on the carbon atoms (see [[McConnell equation]] for details). His theoretical and experimental investigations of the anisotropic nuclear hyperfine interactions  laid a firm foundation for the analysis of the paramagnetic resonance spectra of organic free radicals in. molecular crystals. His work also provided the first experimental demonstration of 
a negative spin density at a proton. He also realized that certain nitric oxide free radicals had the potential of providing labels for studying molecular motions. His introduction of 'spin labels' has led to a deep understanding of such motions, and to extensive applications in many biological systems of great interest. These motions include the rates of translational diffusion of lipids in bilayer membranes as well as the rates of trans membrane phospholipid "flip-flop". In fact nitric oxide free radical "spin labels" provided some of the earliest evidence for the fluidity of biological membranes.<ref name="Hayes"/><ref name="Thomas">{{cite journal|author1=David D. Thomas |author2=Betty J. Gaffney |author3=O.Hayes Griffith |title=Harden M. McConnell: The Science Speaks for Itself|journal=Biophysical Journal|volume=64|issue=3|pages=573–960|date=March 1993|doi=10.1016/S0006-3495(93)81415-2 |pmid=19431875 |bibcode=1993BpJ....64..573T|pmc=1262368}}</ref>

His later research was concerned with the physical chemistry of biological membranes. These studies range all the way from lipid monolayers at the air-water interface to the regions of membrane-membrane contact that are important in immunology. An important contribution was the introduction of supported lipid bilayers to mimic cell surfaces. For example, this system was used to mimic antigen presentation whereby a specific molecule of the major histocompatibility complex is incorporated into the bilayer, a specific antigenic peptide is added, and the combined system used to stimulate a specific T - helper cell.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Harden McConnell|year=2010|title=Adventures in Physical Chemistry|journal=Annual Review of Biophysics|volume=39|pages=1–21|doi=10.1146/annurev.biophys.093008.131315|pmid=20462374}}</ref>

In 1983 McConnell founded Molecular Devices Corporation along with three former graduate students and post docs (Gillian Humphries, j. Wallace Parce and Dean Hafeman) together with a talented engineer, Calvin Chow. The company produced instrumentation for biochemical analysis and drug discovery. The company had over 1,000 employees when it was acquired in 2007. McConnell served on the board of directors between 1983 and 2007.<ref>[http://hardenmcconnell.org/addendum_I_MDC.html hardenmcconnell.org > Addendum I: Molecular Devices Corporation] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702071922/http://hardenmcconnell.org/addendum_I_MDC.html |date=2020-07-02 }} (accessed October 11, 2014)</ref>

"The majority of the 150 scientists who worked with Harden as graduate students, postdocs, and senior colleagues, attended a symposium on April 4, 1992, at Stanford University, in celebration of Harden's 65th birthday.  As an outgrowth of that symposium, these scientists organized special issues of the ''Biophysical Journal''<ref>[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/00063495/64/3 ''Biophysical Journal'' Volume 64, Issue 3, Pages 573-960 (March 1993)] (This issue is made freely available as part of this journal's Open Archive.) (accessed October 11, 2014).</ref> and ''The Journal of Physical Chemistry''<ref>[http://pubs.acs.org/toc/jpchax/97/12 The Journal of Physical Chemistry, Volume 97, Issue 12, Pages 2805-3075, March 1, 1993] (accessed October 11, 2014)</ref> to present current aspects of their work and his. Several other scientists whose work has been influenced by McConnell's contributed articles also.  The symposium and these papers provide powerful testimony to the profound impact that Harden McConnell has had in the fields of chemical physics, molecular biophysics, and cellular biophysics.  McConnell's influence comes not only from his own impressive publication list, but also from the scores of scientists whose careers he has inspired, by his example of intellectual brilliance, and personal integrity."<ref name="Thomas"/>  "The McConnell Book: Biographical Sketches and Memoirs of Students and Lab Associates in Celebration of Harden M. McConnell's 65th Birthday," was also published.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/2849966|title=The McConnell book: biographical sketches and memoirs of students and lab associates in celebration of Harden M. McConnell's 65th birthday, 1992|editor-first=Harden M.|editor-last=McConnell|date=May 21, 1992|publisher=s.n.]|via=Library Catalog (Blacklight)}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
He was awarded the [[Wolf Prize in Chemistry]] in 1983/84 for "his studies of the electronic structure of molecules through paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy and for the introduction and biological applications of spin label techniques".<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.wolffund.org.il/cat.asp?id=15&cat_title=CHEMISTRY|title=The Wolf Prize in Chemistry|access-date=2007-08-26|archive-date=2007-05-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070517203044/http://www.wolffund.org.il/cat.asp?id=15&cat_title=CHEMISTRY|url-status=dead}}</ref>

He has also received several [[awards]] and [[wiktionary:honours|honours]]. Following are the [[awards]] and honours received by Dr. McConnell.

==Personal life==
Harden M. McConnell was born on July 18, 1927, in Richmond, Virginia, and his interest in science, particularly chemistry, began when he discovered a box of copper sulfate crystals in the basement of his home at the approximate age of 12. He died on Wednesday, October 8, 2014  at his home in [[Atherton, California]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2014/10/harden-mcconnell-distinguished-chemistry-professor-stanford-dies|title=Harden McConnell, distinguished chemistry professor at Stanford, dies|website=news.stanford.edu}}</ref>
